divinemc.summary: Multi-functional fork of Purpur, which focuses on the flexibility of your server and its optimization.
divinemc.tagline: A Purpur fork that puts every core to work
divinemc.lede: Spreads chunks, worlds and entity work across your CPU cores, so a busy server keeps its tick rate. Swap your previous jar: every setting stays, and your Bukkit, Spigot and Paper plugins run as they are.

regionized-chunk-ticking.title: Regionized chunk ticking
regionized-chunk-ticking.body: Chunks tick in parallel across regions, similar to how Folia does it, without giving up plugin compatibility.

parallel-world-ticking.title: Parallel world ticking
parallel-world-ticking.body: Each world ticks on its own thread, so the Nether and the End stop queueing behind the overworld.

parallel-sensor-phase.title: Parallel sensor phase
parallel-sensor-phase.body: The expensive read-only part of mob AI — entity scans, line-of-sight checks — runs on a thread pool.

raytrace-entity-culling.title: Raytrace entity culling
raytrace-entity-culling.body: Entities a player provably cannot see are never sent, saving bandwidth and blinding entity-ESP cheats.

async-operations.title: Async operations
async-operations.body: Pathfinding, the entity tracker, mob spawning, joining, chunk sending and portal pre-loading move off the main thread.

secure-seed.title: Secure seed
secure-seed.body: A 1024-bit seed in place of the standard 64-bit one, so structures and ores cannot be cracked from the world.

linear-region-format.title: Linear region format
linear-region-format.body: Store worlds in the V1/V2 linear format or the new buffered one instead of Anvil.

mod-protocols.title: Mod protocols
mod-protocols.body: Server-side support for Syncmatica, AppleSkin, Jade and Xaero's Map.

sentry-integration.title: Sentry integration
sentry-integration.body: Detailed error tracking and monitoring, originally from Pufferfish.

run-a-server.label: Run a server
run-a-server.title: Download the jar
run-a-server.body: Grab the latest build and start it with the command below. DivineMC needs Java 25 or newer.

build-a-plugin.label: Build a plugin
build-a-plugin.title: Compile against the API
build-a-plugin.body: The DivineMC API is a superset of Paper’s, published to the BX Team snapshots repository.

quark.summary: Small modular framework for Minecraft plugins: runtime dependencies, annotated configs, update checks and dev servers.
quark.tagline: The parts every plugin needs, as modules you pick
quark.lede: Download dependencies when the plugin starts, keep configs in annotated classes, check for updates and run a test server straight from Gradle. Every module is optional and relocated into your own package.

runtime-dependencies.title: Runtime dependencies
runtime-dependencies.body: Libraries are downloaded, resolved transitively and loaded when the plugin starts, so the jar stays small.

relocation.title: Relocation
relocation.body: Quark and your libraries move into the plugin’s package, so the server’s own copy of Gson or Guava never wins.

annotated-configs.title: Annotated configs
annotated-configs.body: Plain classes saved as YAML in field order, with comments, validation, migrations and Bukkit types.

update-checks.title: Update checks
update-checks.body: Modrinth, Hangar, GitHub, SpigotMC or any JSON endpoint, with a console message and a join notification.

platform-adapters.title: Platform adapters
platform-adapters.body: One Platform and Scheduler API for Paper, Folia, Bukkit, Velocity and BungeeCord.

gradle-plugin.title: Gradle plugin
gradle-plugin.body: Picks the adapter and modules, configures Shadow and starts a dev server with your plugin and others.

gradle.label: Gradle
gradle.title: Apply the plugin
gradle.body: Pick the platform and the modules you need, then declare runtime dependencies in the quark configuration.

dev-server.label: Dev server
dev-server.title: Run a test server
dev-server.body: Quark downloads the server, installs your plugin and the plugins you list, and starts it in your terminal.

ndailyrewards.summary: Simple and lightweight plugin that allows you to reward your players for playing on your server every day.
ndailyrewards.tagline: Reward players for coming back every day
ndailyrewards.lede: A daily reward streak with a GUI you can reshape completely, MariaDB or SQLite storage, and actions for anything a reward should do.

mariadb-and-sqlite.title: MariaDB and SQLite
mariadb-and-sqlite.body: Keep streaks in a local SQLite file or share them across a network through MariaDB.

custom-gui.title: Custom GUI
custom-gui.body: Every slot of the reward menu is configurable, including custom model data, item models and player heads.

reward-actions.title: Reward actions
reward-actions.body: Commands, messages, sounds and more — a reward is a list of actions, not a fixed item.

placeholderapi.title: PlaceholderAPI
placeholderapi.body: Streaks, cooldowns and claim state exposed as placeholders for scoreboards and menus.

join-notifications.title: Join notifications
join-notifications.body: Remind players on join, or open the reward menu for them automatically, and claim on their behalf if you prefer.

time-management.title: Time management
time-management.body: Flexible cooldowns and reset times, with MiniMessage and ampersand colour codes in every message.

install.label: Install
install.title: Drop it into plugins/
install.body: Download from Modrinth or Hangar, put the jar in your plugins folder and restart. Spigot, Paper and Paper-based forks are supported.

developer-api.label: Developer API
developer-api.title: Listen to its events
developer-api.body: NDailyRewards is published to the BX Team releases repository.

riven.summary: Native Minecraft launcher and modpack toolkit in pure Rust.
riven.tagline: A Minecraft launcher that builds packs too
riven.lede: Install a modpack from a link and get its updates on every launch — or build your own in the app or the CLI, publish it to GitHub Pages and run it headless on a server.

full-launcher.title: Full launcher
full-launcher.body: Instances, Microsoft and offline accounts, automatic Java, Vanilla, Fabric, Quilt, NeoForge and Forge.

packs-from-a-link.title: Packs from a link
packs-from-a-link.body: Modrinth modpacks, .mrpack, Prism exports and Riven packs; a pack updates itself before every launch.

developer-mode.title: Developer mode
developer-mode.body: Content table, dependency tree, config editor, releases, git and a test instance in one window.

signed-fast-updates.title: Signed, fast updates
signed-fast-updates.body: Release channels, a tiny pointer checked with ETag, content-addressed downloads and ed25519 signatures pinned on first install — no keys in links.

servers.title: Servers
servers.body: riven install --side server --headless keeps a dedicated server on the latest release.

nix-without-packhash.title: Nix without packHash
nix-without-packhash.body: lib.mkModpack fetches every file by the hash in riven.json — no fixed-output hash to bump.

nyx.summary: Modern, lightweight desktop GUI for the Mihomo proxy core.
nyx.tagline: A desktop client for Mihomo, in pure Rust
nyx.lede: Manage profiles, proxy groups, rules and connections from a clean interface — with system proxy and TUN mode, a connection inspector and a built-in profile editor.

system-proxy-and-tun.title: System proxy and TUN
system-proxy-and-tun.body: Route one app or the whole machine; a helper service handles TUN mode after a one-time elevation.

connection-inspector.title: Connection inspector
connection-inspector.body: Live connections grouped per process, with app icons, so you can see what is going where.

profile-editor.title: Profile editor
profile-editor.body: Edit profiles, proxy groups and rules in the app instead of hand-editing YAML.

installer-or-portable.title: Installer or portable
installer-or-portable.body: Windows installer or zip; deb, rpm, Arch package or a tarball on Linux.

nix-flake.title: Nix flake
nix-flake.body: Run it with nix run, or use the NixOS module, which declares the service so TUN works without a password prompt.

lightweight.title: Lightweight
lightweight.body: A single native gpui application — no Electron, no bundled browser.

download.label: Download
download.title: Grab a release
download.body: Installers and portable builds for Windows and Linux are attached to every GitHub release.

vanilla-reimagined.summary: Fabric mods that heavily optimise the game and bring back OptiFine features.
vanilla-reimagined.tagline: Vanilla, faster, with the OptiFine features back
vanilla-reimagined.lede: A Fabric modpack built to optimise the game as much as possible and to bring back what people installed OptiFine for, without changing how vanilla plays.

performance.title: Performance
performance.body: Sodium, Lithium, Moonrise, FerriteCore, ImmediatelyFast, Entity Culling and Dynamic FPS.

visual-features.title: Visual features
visual-features.body: Iris for shaders, dynamic lights from LambDynamicLights and Sodium Extra’s video options.

optifine-like-features.title: OptiFine-like features
optifine-like-features.body: Zoom, connected textures, custom entity models and textures, and OptiGUI for resource-pack GUIs.

quality-of-life.title: Quality of life
quality-of-life.body: Mod Menu, no reloading screen and the config screens to tune all of it.

contribute.body: The pack is built with Riven; the repository explains how to add mods, change configs and test it.

smallHeap.title: Heap under 2 GB
smallHeap.body: A modern server barely boots in this much. These sets assume 4 GB and up; below that the GC tuning is noise.

compressedOops.title: Compressed references stop working near 32 GB
compressedOops.body: Above roughly 32 GB the JVM drops compressed object pointers, so every reference doubles in size. A 31 GB heap often holds more objects than a 33 GB one.

zgcSmallHeap.title: ZGC below its intended heap
zgcSmallHeap.body: This set is meant for 32 GB or more on 10+ cores. On a smaller host G1 collects less often and leaves more CPU for ticks.

zgcCores.title: ZGC needs spare cores
zgcCores.body: ZGC collects concurrently, so it competes with the server threads for CPU. On a busy box that shows up as lower TPS, not as pauses.

noGraal.title: Nothing here uses GraalVM
noGraal.body: {preset} has no Graal-specific options. Pick MeowIce or brucethemoose to get them.

graalPrefix.title: Graal properties use the new prefix
graalPrefix.body: From Java 23 the compiler reads -Djdk.graal.*; the old -Dgraal.* names are ignored without an error.

x86Dropped.title: x86-only options were left out
x86Dropped.body: An aarch64 JVM rejects -XX:+UseXmm*, -XX:UseAVX and the other x86 intrinsics outright and refuses to start, so they are not in this list.

biasedLocking.title: -XX:-UseBiasedLocking was left out
biasedLocking.body: Biased locking was removed in Java 18 and the option is now rejected. It is only emitted for Java 17.

shenandoahIu.title: Shenandoah iu mode was left out
shenandoahIu.body: The incremental-update mode is gone in Java 24; the default (SATB) mode is used instead.

compactHeaders.title: Compact object headers are on
compactHeaders.body: Java 24 can store an object header in 8 bytes instead of 12. Expect a few percent less heap for the same world.

largePagesLinux.title: Large pages need the host configured
largePagesLinux.body: Without transparent huge pages enabled (or vm.nr_hugepages reserved) the JVM prints a warning at startup and falls back to normal pages.

largePages.title: Large pages need the host configured
largePages.body: Outside Linux large pages need an OS privilege (SeLockMemoryPrivilege on Windows). Without it the JVM warns at startup and carries on with normal pages.

vectorIncubator.title: The Vector API is still incubating
vectorIncubator.body: Java prints a warning about an incubator module on every start. That line is expected, not a misconfiguration.

javaTooOld.title: Too old for current server builds
javaTooOld.body: Current Paper builds need Java 21, and DivineMC needs Java 25.

divinemcJava.title: DivineMC needs Java 25
divinemcJava.body: Paper and Purpur still run on Java 21, but current DivineMC builds refuse to start below 25.

coords.name: Coordinate calculator
coords.description: Convert coordinates between the Nether and the Overworld, and find a stronghold from two Eye of Ender throws.
coords.lead: Line a Nether portal up with its Overworld side, or find a stronghold from two Eye of Ender throws.
coords.portalsLede: One block in the Nether is eight in the Overworld. Y stays the same.
coords.strongholdLede: Two throws, each with your position and the angle you faced. The lines cross at the stronghold.
coords.distance: {n} block from the second throw | {n} blocks from the second throw
coords.shallow: The throws are nearly parallel, so the estimate is rough. Move further sideways for the second one.
coords.parallel: The two throws point the same way. Walk sideways a few hundred blocks and throw again.
coords.behind: The lines cross behind you. Check that both angles were read while facing the eye.
coords.how1: Throw an Eye of Ender, look straight at it and open F3. Write down X and Z from {xyz} and the first number from {facing}.
coords.how2: Walk 250 to 500 blocks to the side — not towards the eye — and do the same again. The wider the angle between the two lines, the closer the result.
coords.how3: Go to the coordinates above and throw one more eye to confirm. When it falls, you are standing over the stronghold.
